title: HE CURSED THE KING, THREW STONES AT HIM, AND WALKED AWAY ALIVE. WHY DID DAVID LET HIM?
paragraphs: HE CURSED THE KING, THREW STONES AT HIM, AND WALKED AWAY ALIVE. WHY DID DAVID LET HIM?

The shocking story of Shimei reveals what happens when a wounded heart has the power to retaliate—but chooses to leave judgment in God's hands. And the deeper truth may expose something you've been carrying for years.
There are some people you can forgive in your prayers… until you hear their voice again.
Until somebody mentions their name.
Until you remember what they said when you were already struggling to survive.
And suddenly, the wound you thought had healed begins bleeding all over again.
You remember the humiliation. The betrayal. The people who believed the lies. The ones who stood there watching while your reputation was being torn apart.
And somewhere deep inside, a question begins to rise.
Lord, why should they get away with what they did to me?
Now imagine being a king.
You have soldiers who would kill at your command. You have loyal men ready to defend your honor. You possess enough authority to silence the person humiliating you.
And yet, instead of ordering their execution, you lower your head and keep walking.
That is exactly what happened to David.
But here is what makes this story almost unbearable.
The man cursing David was attacking him at one of the lowest moments of his life. And David knew that some of the pain behind those accusations touched a much darker story about his own past.
This was not simply a lesson about controlling anger.
This was a broken father, a disgraced king, and a guilty man walking through the consequences of decisions he could never undo.
And what David said next would reveal something extraordinary about the difference between defending your pride and surrendering your pain to God.
The story begins in 2 Samuel 16:5–14.
David was fleeing Jerusalem.
Not because a foreign army had conquered his kingdom.
Not because an enemy nation had overwhelmed his defenses.
He was running because his own son, Absalom, had turned against him.
Think about that.
The child David had once held in his arms had become the man threatening his throne.
The boy he had watched grow up was now leading a rebellion that could cost him his life.
David was not merely losing political power.
He was watching his family collapse.
He had already crossed the Kidron Valley. He had climbed the Mount of Olives, weeping, with his head covered and his feet bare (2 Samuel 15:30).
Imagine those footsteps.
Every step away from Jerusalem was another reminder that the kingdom he had spent years establishing was slipping from his hands.
He was still God's anointed king.
But he looked nothing like a victorious ruler.
He looked like a father who had lost his son.
A man who had lost his home.
A sinner who could not escape the memory of his own failures.
And then, just when the road seemed cruel enough, another man appeared.
His name was Shimei, son of Gera, from the family of Saul.
He did not come to comfort David.
He came to curse him.
Scripture says:
"And he cast stones at David, and at all the servants of king David: and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left."
— 2 Samuel 16:6, KJV
Picture the scene.
A weary king walking down a dusty road.
His loyal soldiers surrounding him.
The sound of stones striking the ground.
Dust rising.
A voice shouting accusations from the hillside.
And Shimei was not whispering.
He was publicly humiliating David.
He cried:
"Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial."
— 2 Samuel 16:7, KJV
In the Hebrew text, Shimei calls David אִישׁ הַדָּמִים (ish haddamim), meaning a man of bloodshed, and אִישׁ הַבְּלִיָּעַל (ish habbeliyya'al), an expression describing a wicked or worthless man.
These were not harmless insults.
Shimei was accusing David of being a violent, morally corrupt ruler who deserved to lose everything.
He went further, claiming that the LORD had returned upon David the bloodshed associated with Saul's house and had given the kingdom to Absalom (2 Samuel 16:8).
But there is something important we must understand.
Shimei's accusation was not automatically true simply because David refused to retaliate.

The biblical account does not establish Shimei's charge that David murdered his way into Saul's throne. In fact, David had repeatedly refused opportunities to kill Saul (1 Samuel 24; 26), and he had mourned Saul's death.
Shimei was speaking from hostility and resentment.
His accusation distorted David's history.
Yet David was not innocent of all bloodguilt.
Years earlier, David had committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged the death of her husband, Uriah.
The prophet Nathan had confronted him.
David had confessed.
God had forgiven him, but Nathan also announced painful consequences that would affect his household (2 Samuel 12:9–13).
And now David was walking through a family rebellion.
Shimei's particular accusation against David concerning Saul's house was not established as true.
But David knew he was not a sinless man.
That distinction changes the way we understand his response.
Sometimes the person attacking you is wrong about what happened.
Sometimes their accusations are unfair.
Sometimes their motives are cruel.
But even then, the experience can remind you of places in your life where you genuinely need God's mercy.
Not every criticism is God's verdict.
Not every accusation is true.
And not every painful event is a punishment for a particular sin.
But a humble heart remains willing to examine itself before the Lord.
Then came the moment when everything could have turned bloody.
Abishai, one of David's warriors, had heard enough.
He was furious.
He could not understand why the king would tolerate such humiliation.
So he asked:
"Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? let me go over, I pray thee, and take off his head."
— 2 Samuel 16:9, KJV
Abishai was ready to end the confrontation immediately.
One command.
One sword.
One dead man.
And the insults would stop.
David had the power to make it happen.
Nobody would have needed to convince Abishai.
He was already willing.
But David said no.
And here is where the story reaches into places we do not always want God to touch.
Because sometimes our greatest spiritual battle is not against the person who wounded us.
It is against the desire to make them feel what they made us feel.
You want them to understand.
You want them embarrassed.
You want them exposed.
You want them to experience the same sleepless nights you endured.
And when the opportunity finally comes to retaliate, something inside whispers:
Now they will know.
But David refused to give that desire control over his next decision.
Listen carefully to his words:
"Let him alone, and let him curse; for the LORD hath bidden him."
— 2 Samuel 16:11, KJV
The Hebrew expression הַנִּחוּ לוֹ (hannichu lo) means, in this context, "Leave him alone."
David was telling his men to stand down.
He was not inviting Shimei to become more abusive.
He was not declaring that Shimei's accusations were righteous.
He was refusing to turn his soldiers into instruments of personal revenge.
David interpreted the humiliation as something God might be permitting within His providential dealings with him.
That is different from saying God morally approved of Shimei's hatred.
Scripture does not teach that every cruel word is a command from heaven or that every abusive person speaks for God.
David's response reveals his own posture of humility before divine sovereignty, not an endorsement of Shimei's wrongdoing.
And then David said something even more astonishing.
"It may be that the LORD will look on mine affliction, and that the LORD will requite me good for his cursing this day."
— 2 Samuel 16:12, KJV
There it is.
The sentence that reveals the heart of this entire encounter.
"It may be."
In Hebrew, the verse begins with אוּלַי (ulay), meaning "perhaps" or "maybe."
David was not claiming to know exactly what God would do.
He was not announcing a guaranteed blessing because he had endured humiliation.
He was expressing hope.
Perhaps God will see.
Perhaps God will show mercy.
Perhaps the Lord will bring good out of this terrible day.
David could not control Shimei's mouth.
He could not force Absalom to love him.
He could not rewrite the decisions that had damaged his family.
But he could entrust his uncertain future to the mercy of God.
And that is where this ancient story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us have been living as though peace cannot begin until the people who hurt us finally admit what they did.
We are waiting for an apology.
Waiting for a confession.
Waiting for somebody to correct the story they told about us.
Waiting for the people who abandoned us to come back and acknowledge the damage.
And while we wait, we keep carrying the injury.
Into our marriages.
Into our friendships.
Into our prayers.
Sometimes even into the way we treat people who had nothing to do with the original wound.
The person who hurt us may have moved on.
But we are still standing on the road, listening to Shimei.
Still rehearsing the argument.
Still imagining the confrontation.
Still trying to win a battle that ended years ago.
And perhaps today the Lord is inviting you to consider a different response.
Not pretending the wrong was acceptable.
Not denying the pain.
Not abandoning justice.
But refusing to let revenge become the ruler of your heart.
David's restraint did not mean he was unaffected.
The text says Shimei continued along the hillside, cursing, throwing stones, and scattering dust as David and his men traveled.
The humiliation did not immediately stop.
There was no sudden apology.
No dramatic reconciliation.
No crowd cheering for David's patience.
Verse 14 simply tells us that the king and the people with him arrived weary and refreshed themselves.
That detail matters.
They were exhausted.
David's obedience did not make the road painless.
He still had to walk it.
And some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You have prayed.
You have tried to forgive.
You have chosen not to retaliate.
But the consequences of what happened are still there.
You still have to rebuild trust.
You still have to live with losses.
You still wake up some mornings remembering what you wish you could forget.
Please hear this.
Forgiveness is not proof that the wound never mattered. It is a refusal to make revenge the purpose of your life.
And forgiveness does not require returning to danger, concealing abuse, refusing lawful protection, or allowing an unrepentant person unlimited access to your life.
David's example is not a command to remain silent in the face of every injustice.
There are times to establish boundaries.
There are times to seek help.
There are times to report wrongdoing and pursue accountability.
But even while pursuing what is right, we must guard our hearts against becoming consumed by vengeance.
The apostle Paul later wrote:
"Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."
— Romans 12:19, KJV
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say evil is harmless.
It does not say justice is unnecessary.
It says personal vengeance belongs in hands far greater than ours.
And that brings us to something many readers miss when they first encounter Shimei.
David did not simply forget what happened.
When Absalom's rebellion ended and David returned toward Jerusalem, Shimei hurried to meet him and acknowledged his wrongdoing.
Abishai again wanted him executed.
Again David refused.
This time David swore that Shimei would not die that day (2 Samuel 19:16–23).
But the story did not end there.

Near the end of his life, David spoke to Solomon about Shimei and his earlier curse. He reminded Solomon of his oath not to kill Shimei himself and instructed him to deal wisely with the matter (1 Kings 2:8–9).
Later, Solomon placed Shimei under a specific restriction. After Shimei violated that royal command, Solomon ordered his execution (1 Kings 2:36–46).
This is an uncomfortable ending.
And we must not hide it just to make David's earlier restraint sound more beautiful.
David's initial refusal to punish Shimei was real.
His later instructions concerning Shimei are also part of Scripture.
The Bible does not present David as a flawless example of forgiveness in every subsequent decision.
It gives us the life of a complicated man who experienced mercy, exercised restraint, committed serious sins, and still needed grace.
That is why we must be careful not to turn this account into a simplistic promise that every enemy will eventually become a friend or that every injustice will be resolved exactly as we desire.
The historical narrative is more complicated.
And perhaps that makes it more honest.
Because our own lives are complicated too.
We sometimes show mercy beautifully in one season and struggle with resentment in another.
We surrender something to God, only to discover later that we are still holding part of it.
We forgive in prayer and then feel anger return when a memory resurfaces.
We love Jesus, but we are still learning how to live like Him.
David's story is not ultimately an invitation to admire David as a perfect man.
It is an invitation to recognize how desperately even a king after God's own heart needed a greater King.
And that King is Jesus Christ.
Centuries after David walked away from Shimei's curses, another King would be publicly humiliated.
He too would be rejected.
He too would endure false accusations.
He too would be surrounded by people who mocked His kingship.
But unlike David, Jesus had no personal sin to confess.
He was completely righteous.
He did not deserve the humiliation.
He did not deserve the suffering.
He did not deserve the cross.
Yet He endured it.
The Gospel of Luke records His prayer:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
— Luke 23:34, KJV
In Greek, the opening words are:
Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς (Pater, aphes autois)
"Father, forgive them."
The verb ἄφες (aphes) comes from aphiēmi, a verb used for releasing, letting go, or forgiving.

There is a textual detail worth acknowledging: this saying is absent from some early Greek manuscripts of Luke, while it is preserved in others and in the traditional text underlying the King James Version. It has long been received as part of the Christian reading of Jesus' crucifixion.
And the mercy it expresses is consistent with the teaching and character of Christ throughout the New Testament.
But do not miss the difference between David and Jesus.
David was a sinful king hoping for mercy.
Jesus is the sinless King through whom mercy is offered.
David could refuse to punish an offender on a particular day.
Jesus could accomplish what David never could: bear the sins of His people and reconcile them to God.
David's restraint did not remove the guilt of humanity.
Christ's sacrifice addresses sin at its deepest level.
As Peter writes of Jesus:
— 1 Peter 2:23, KJV
Read that again.
He committed Himself to the One who judges righteously.
That is the heart of Christian surrender.
Not the belief that evil does not matter.
But the confidence that God is righteous, even when we cannot immediately see justice.
And the same Jesus who endured injustice also calls sinners to repentance.
Because we are not always David on the road.
Sometimes we are Shimei on the hillside.
Sometimes we are the ones throwing stones.
Not literal stones, perhaps.
But words.
Accusations.
Cruel comments.
Rumors.
Mockery.
Judgments made without understanding the whole story.
Sometimes we have wounded people who were already struggling.
Sometimes we have enjoyed seeing somebody fall.
Sometimes we have justified our bitterness because we believed our anger made us righteous.
And when we look honestly at ourselves, we discover that we do not merely need protection from the cruelty of others.
We need forgiveness for the cruelty that can exist in our own hearts.
That is why the Gospel is such extraordinary news.
Jesus did not come merely to teach wounded people how to cope with pain.
He came to save sinners.
To reconcile rebels to God.
To forgive the guilty.
To transform hearts that cannot repair themselves.
The cross exposes both the seriousness of our sin and the astonishing depth of God's love.
And the resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not because God pretends the scandal never happened.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem people whose stories have been marked by guilt, shame, betrayal, and ruin.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a wound nobody knows about.
Maybe your own family has become the source of your deepest sorrow.
Maybe you have been falsely accused.
Maybe someone you trusted betrayed you.
Or maybe the Holy Spirit is confronting you with something harder.
Maybe you were the one who betrayed the trust.
Maybe you were the one who spoke carelessly.
Maybe you were the one who damaged a relationship and then convinced yourself you were justified.
Whatever side of the story you are on, the invitation of Jesus remains.
Come into the light.
Repent where you have sinned.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Pursue what is right where injustice has occurred.
And entrust your heart to the Savior who knows the whole truth.
You do not have to pretend you are healed when you are not.
You do not have to call evil good.
You do not have to earn God's mercy by suffering silently.
And you do not have to keep feeding the bitterness that has been consuming you.
The grace of Christ is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is the power and invitation to begin a new life in Him.
Perhaps the most difficult question in David's story is not why he allowed Shimei to keep speaking.
Perhaps it is this:
What would happen if you stopped letting the person who wounded you determine the person you are becoming?
What would change in your home?
In your prayers?
In your relationships?
In the way you speak about people who disappointed you?
What if your next decision were governed not by the memory of their cruelty, but by the truth of Christ's mercy?
That does not mean healing will happen overnight.
Some wounds require time, wise counsel, safety, and ongoing support.
But you can begin by bringing your pain honestly before God.
You can tell Him that you are angry.
You can tell Him you are exhausted.
You can confess that part of you still wants revenge.
You can ask Him to make you willing to forgive, even when your emotions have not caught up with your prayers.
And if you are the one who needs to repent, do not hide behind religious language.
Tell the truth.
Take responsibility.
Make amends where possible.
Seek reconciliation without demanding that someone immediately trust you again.
Because biblical repentance is not merely feeling sorry that you were exposed.
It is turning toward God and bearing fruit consistent with that change.
And when you cannot carry the weight of your failures any longer, remember the promise of 1 John 1:9:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
This is the hope of the Gospel.
Not that our past was harmless.
Not that the people we wounded were unaffected.
Not that consequences always disappear.
But that forgiveness and transformation are possible through Jesus Christ.
Maybe today you need to stop rehearsing an old argument.
Maybe you need to make a phone call.
Maybe you need to apologize.
Maybe you need to establish a boundary you have been afraid to set.
Maybe you need to kneel beside your bed and finally tell God how deeply something hurt.
Whatever the next faithful step looks like, take it with Christ.
Because the road David walked was covered in dust and humiliation.
But the road to the cross was marked by a greater suffering and a greater mercy.
And the risen Jesus is able to meet you on the road you are walking today.
If this message has exposed a wound, a struggle, or a sin you have been hiding, I want to invite you into an honest moment before God.
You do not need to publish the details of your pain.
There is no shame in asking your brothers and sisters in Christ to pray.
You may be surprised how many people reading these words have walked through something similar.
And perhaps your honest response will remind someone else that they are not alone.
Return to 2 Samuel 16:5–14.
Remember David's restraint, his uncertainty, his need for mercy, and the greater King who came after him.
Not simply to increase the reach of a page, but because someone among your family, friends, coworkers, or acquaintances may be carrying bitterness, grief, shame, or guilt in silence.
Someone may be ready to retaliate.
Someone may be struggling to forgive.
Someone may need to be reminded that Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
A thoughtful share can place Scripture before someone who might never have searched for it themselves.
And if this ministry has helped you grow in your understanding of God's Word, I want to invite you to consider taking a deeper step with us.

Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim the Gospel, encourage repentance, strengthen believers, and help people move beyond superficial inspiration into a deeper understanding of Scripture and a closer walk with Jesus Christ.
But continuing and expanding that work requires real resources.
Behind every article, every devotional, every discipleship resource, and every effort to reach another soul is a ministry that needs faithful support.

For those who choose to give as part of their Christian stewardship, that support can be an expression of generosity and an offering toward the work of spreading biblical truth. It should not be confused with a required church tithe or treated as a substitute for responsibilities to your local church.
Scripture reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That is the spirit in which we ask.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not the promise of special blessings in exchange for money.
But an opportunity to participate willingly in a ministry devoted to making Jesus known.
These products are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply another way to share faith-centered messages, encourage discipleship, and express appreciation to those helping sustain the ministry.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage people to read Scripture for themselves.

Our desire is that people would not merely read another emotional message and move on, but would become more deeply rooted in God's Word, more discerning in truth, more faithful in repentance, and more devoted to the Lord Jesus Christ.
It is not a viral post.
It is not the number of comments beneath an article.
It is seeing people turn to Christ, grow in grace, and learn to walk in obedience to His Word.
And before you leave, I want you to think about one final scene.
A king walking down a dusty road.
A wounded father with tears behind his eyes.
A bitter man throwing stones.
A soldier waiting for permission to draw his sword.
And David saying, in effect, Leave him alone.
Now think of another King.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Crowned with thorns.
Hanging upon a cross.
Not because He had lost control.
But because He had come to accomplish the redemption that sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
David needed God's mercy.
Shimei needed God's mercy.
Abishai needed God's mercy.
And so do we.
The question is no longer simply whether somebody has thrown stones at you.
The question is whether you will bring both your wounds and your sins to the feet of Jesus.
Because you can spend the rest of your life trying to make someone pay for what they did.
Or you can begin walking with the Savior who paid the price for sin at Calvary.
Do not let the stones they threw become the walls that keep your heart from the grace of Christ.
